title: Leon Black sues to block House subpoenas on Epstein payments; skips deposition on September 3
dek: Private equity investor Leon Black filed a federal lawsuit Thursday to block House Oversight Committee subpoenas demanding testimony and documents about his financial relationship with Jeffrey Epstein, and failed to appear for a scheduled deposition the same day. Black has paid Epstein between $158 million and $180 million, according to different sources, and faces potential contempt of Congress proceedings.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: Black paid Epstein $158-180 million and is now challenging Congressional subpoenas through federal court rather than complying with deposition demands.
bottom_line: A federal judge must now decide whether Black's privacy and NDA claims shield him from Congressional compulsion or whether the House's investigative authority prevails. The outcome will determine whether the committee can force Black's testimony before the current Congress adjourns, and it will establish precedent for how courts weigh executive confidentiality against legislative oversight of a billionaire's ties to a convicted sex trafficker.
body:
Private equity investor Leon Black filed a federal lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia on Thursday, September 3, to block House Oversight Committee subpoenas demanding his testimony and documents about his financial relationship with Jeffrey Epstein. Black did not appear for a scheduled deposition that same day.
The lawsuit escalates a months-long legal clash over Congressional access to Black's records and testimony. Black paid Epstein between $158 million and $180 million, according to different accounts. An independent investigation commissioned by Apollo, the private equity firm Black founded, concluded the $158 million covered tax, estate-planning, and other legitimate activities. The Senate Finance Committee, according to ABC News reporting, put the figure at more than $170 million for "tax and estate planning advice." Rep. Robert Garcia cited over $180 million in his public statements.
The House Oversight Committee issued the subpoenas in June after Black appeared for a transcribed interview and refused to answer questions about nondisclosure agreements. Black walked out of that session when asked about NDAs he may have signed.
Black's lawsuit argues the subpoenas exceed the committee's delegated authority and seek private information bearing no legitimate connection to a legislative purpose. His attorney, Susan Estrich, stated in a written filing: "This is no longer about finding the truth about Epstein. It is about trying to destroy Mr. Black. We were left with no choice but to file this lawsuit in response to an abuse of Congressional power." Black's legal team contends the subpoenas would "expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein, who bargained for confidentiality and have refused to release it."
According to Black's lawsuit, he has already "produced the only confidentiality agreement in which Epstein could have been involved" because it is the only one executed while Epstein was alive. Black argues the committee is on a "fishing expedition" that oversteps its authority.
Black testified in June that he has "never abused a woman, never been with an underage woman, never engaged in sex trafficking, never paid Epstein for access to women, and never was blackmailed by Epstein." Black stated he did not know about Epstein's "nefarious activity until Epstein was charged with trafficking in July 2019." Black has denied wrongdoing and maintained a social relationship with Epstein since the mid-1990s, according to ABC News reporting. The House committee has questioned whether Black's payments to Epstein, which served as a lifeline to the convicted sex offender in the years after Epstein's 2008 prison sentence for soliciting a minor for prostitution, warrant investigation.
Chairman James Comer said: "It's a shame Leon Black is hiding behind litigation rather than provide answers to the American people. Mr. Black's testimony is crucial to our investigation." Comer added: "I would hold him in contempt right now. Of all the powerful billionaires and political people we brought in for interviews and depositions, this is the first time anyone's filed suit." He noted the committee is racing against time before the congressional session ends: "Obviously, we're running up against the clock at the end of this Congress, I'm sure his legal team knows that. So we've got to be smart from here on in."
Rep. Garcia called Black's refusal to testify "defying two Congressional subpoenas" and stated: "We must hold him in contempt immediately." Garcia also said: "What he's trying to do is to slow the process down of getting us the information. He's very aware that Comer no longer is going to be the chairperson. But what Mr. Black should understand is that we will be even more aggressive than Chairman Comer as it relates to his testimony."
Black appears in Justice Department Epstein files thousands of times, per NPR reporting, though appearing in the files is not necessarily an indication of criminal wrongdoing. The House committee has questioned Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Bill Gates, Les Wexner, Bill and Hillary Clinton, Epstein's former accountant Richard Kahn, and former attorney Darren Indyke. Epstein's accountant testified that Black was among five clients who paid money to Epstein, according to Comer's statement. The other four on that list reported by NPR were Les Wexner, Steven Sinofsky (former Microsoft Windows Division President), Glenn Dubin (hedge fund investor), and the Rothschild family.
Additional complications arise from Black's history with NDAs.  According to a lawsuit filed by Ganieva against Black, he prepared a nondisclosure agreement in 2015 to secure her silence; the lawsuit was later dismissed. A judge dismissed Ganieva's lawsuit, citing the NDA she signed and about $9 million that she had received in the years after entering the agreement. Files released by the U.S. Justice Department show that Epstein offered Black advice, including suggesting in an email to his assistant that Black hire former law enforcement officers to approach Ganieva. Black's attorney Estrich has dismissed Ganieva's accusation as "demonstrably false." Black has previously said he was the victim of extortion regarding the Ganieva matter.
Black left Apollo Global Management in 2021, stating at the time that "relentless public attention and media scrutiny" of his ties with Epstein had taken "a toll" on his health.
Black's lawsuit asserts the subpoenas are "invalid to the extent they exceed OGR's delegated authority in seeking private information that bears no legitimate connection to OGR's legislative purpose." Black is seeking declaratory and injunctive relief preventing the committee from compelling compliance. He also argues the committee lacks statutory authority to enforce its subpoenas in federal court.
Contempt of Congress could result in the committee referring Black to the Justice Department for potential prosecution. The committee is expected to decide on next steps in coming days.
